GuardFall Exposes Open-Source AI Coding Agents to Decades-Old Shell Injection Risks

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 10 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The safety check that is supposed to stop an AI coding agent from running a dangerous command can be walked straight past using a shell trick that has been public for decades. New research from&nbsp;Adversa AI, which is named the bypass GuardFall, found it works against ten of the eleven popular open-source coding and computer-use agents the firm tested. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts AI-coding-agent-spawned shells running commands obfuscated to defeat plain-text blocklists: empty-quote/backslash-split binary names (r''m), base64 piped into sh/bash, or benign tools (find/dd) given destructive flags. This is the exact GuardFall evasion shape where bash rewrites the string after the agent's filter inspected it. Rationale: Uses the article's literal GuardFall evasion primitives (empty-quote split like r''m, base64-pipe-to-shell, destructive find/dd flags) anchored to the named open-source agent binaries as parents — the combination of agent-parent + shell-child + obfuscated cmdline is far higher-fidelity than any single clause. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1027.010 T1140 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running a build script that base64-decodes an embedded asset and pipes it to a shell installer
  • CI/dev tooling using find -delete to clean build artifacts
  • dd used for legitimate disk imaging by a sysadmin on a dev box
  • Shell aliases or generated scripts that happen to contain quote-adjacent tokens
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run build","make ","cmake","docker build") and ProcessCommandLine has "-delete")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any base64; confirm the parent is an AI coding agent and whether the session was non-interactive/auto-exec. Identify the repo/working dir the agent was pointed at. 2) Contain: kill the agent + shell processes, revoke and rotate any credentials reachable from $HOME (~/.ssh, ~/.aws), and quarantine the host from prod networks. 3) Hunt: review the triggering repo/PR (especially fork PRs and in-repo config like .aider.conf.yml) for the injected instruction; sweep other dev hosts for the same agent-parent + obfuscated-shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the GuardFall precondition: a named open-source coding agent invoked with an auto-execute / skip-permissions flag (--auto-exec, --auto-run, --auto-test, --yes-always, dangerously-skip-permissions) that then spawns a shell or interpreter non-interactively. This is the unattended configuration that lets an injected command actually run. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit auto-execute flag names (--auto-exec/--auto-run/--auto-test/dangerously-skip-permissions) AND the named agent binaries spawning a shell — the unattended-execution precondition the article says must be true for the attack to land, making it a high-fidelity governance/posture alert. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://www.theregister.com/2026/04/01/claude_code_rule_cap_raises/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Developer using --yes-always on their own local repo for a known refactor
  • Automated test harness invoking the agent with --auto-test against a sandboxed branch
  • Demo/eval scripts running an agent non-interactively in a throwaway container
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ci-runner","build-agent") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--auto-test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the agent run was sanctioned (internal trusted repo vs fork/external) and which repo/working dir it targeted; capture the child shell command lines. 2) Contain: if the repo source is untrusted or unknown, terminate the agent session and disable the auto-execute flag in the relevant wrapper/CI job; isolate the host pending review. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts/CI runners running these agents with auto-exec flags, and correlate forward to credential-file reads or outbound connections from the spawned shells.

AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GuardFall credential-theft payload: a shell or copy/transfer tool spawned by an AI coding agent that reads SSH keys, cloud credentials, or other home-folder secrets. Targets the article's stated impact — stealing 'SSH keys and cloud credentials to anything sitting in your home folder'. Rationale: Combines the article's named agent binaries as parent with the exact credential paths it calls out (SSH keys, AWS/cloud creds in $HOME) referenced by a read/copy/transfer child process — agent-spawned access to ~/.ssh or ~/.aws is well outside normal agent working-dir behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An agent legitimately tasked with configuring git over SSH or deploying via scp reading ~/.ssh/config
  • Developer-driven 'aws configure' or terraform run that the agent shells out to and which touches ~/.aws/credentials
  • Backup or dotfile-sync tooling invoked through the agent's shell
  • Agent reading ~/.docker/config.json to run an authorized image build
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws configure","git@","ssh -T","terraform") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the credential access matched the task the user gave the agent; capture the destination of any subsequent cp/scp/curl. 2) Contain: immediately rotate the specific keys/credentials touched (SSH keypairs, AWS access keys, kube tokens) and revoke sessions; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents/NetworkConnectIP4 from the same shell for outbound exfil shortly after the read, and review the source repo/PR that the agent was operating on.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cat","cp","tar","scp","curl","wget","base64")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.aws/credentials|\.config/gcloud|\.kube/config|\.netrc|\.docker/config\.json"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")

Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout AIDelivery Low
Hunts the GuardFall initial-access vector where a malicious agent config file shipped inside a repository (the article calls out .aider.conf.yml) is written to disk by a VCS/clone or the agent itself, which can trigger the attack on the first accepted edit. Treats in-repo agent config as untrusted code. Rationale: Uses the exact config filename the article names as untrusted-code (.aider.conf.yml) written by a clone/checkout or the agent — a focused hunting pivot for the supply-chain delivery step, kept low-confidence/hunting because legitimate repos also ship this file. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/blog/the-approval-prompt-is-lying-to-you-symlink-rce-in-five-ai-coding-agents-claude-code-cursor-antigravity-copilot-grok-build/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem

  • Templating/scaffolding tools generating an aider config
  • CI checkout of an internal repo that ships the file by policy
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/internal-repos/","/trusted/"))

1) Triage: inspect the contents of the written .aider.conf.yml for embedded auto-run/auto-commit settings, shell hooks, or instructions, and identify the source repo/PR (especially fork PRs). 2) Contain: if the repo is untrusted/external, prevent the agent from running against it, move $HOME to a throwaway folder per the article's guidance, and disable auto-execute. 3) Hunt: correlate forward to agent-spawned shells (UC1/UC2) and credential reads (UC3) on the same host within the session window.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

What the Numbers Say About FIFA 2026 Cyber Risk

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 11 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The FIFA World Cup 2026 opened on June 11. By that date, according to Check Point Research, the fraud infrastructure targeting it had already been built, staged, and partially deployed. Threat actor activity was pre-planned, months out, across three sectors and at least ten languages. Check Point Exposure Management published the FIFA World Cup 2026 Cyber Threat Report this month, covering

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Network/DNS contact with FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike fraud domains · [LLM] Inbound mail or embedded URL from FIFA 2026 impersonation domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Network/DNS contact with FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike fraud domains AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS resolutions and network connections to the specific FIFA 2026 brand-impersonation domains staged by the Check Point / Group-IB-tracked fraud infrastructure (hospitality, store, and gambling lures). Article-specific because it pins the named registered domains rather than a generic 'newly-registered domain' heuristic. Rationale: Uses the seven concrete lookalike domains from the article's IOC bundle (www-fifa.me/.co, 26-fifa.com, op.shop-26fifa.com, fifaofficialstore.shop, fifa2026guess.com, fortune-worldcup2026.com.cn); these are dedicated fraud-only domains so any resolution is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against the FBI IC3 PSA and Check Point's research blog which independently confirm the campaign and several of the same domains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260527 • https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/before-the-first-whistle-how-cyber-criminals-are-targeting-world-cup-2026/ • https://www.gblock.app/articles/fifa-2026-phishing-wave-fake-domains-email-scams
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or threat-intel platform manually browsing the domain during triage
  • Automated URL-detonation sandbox / SOAR enrichment visiting the domain from a known scanning host
  • Secure web gateway pre-fetch or link-rewrite service resolving the URL on the user's behalf
  • Brand-protection / takedown vendor crawling the domain from corporate ranges
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-sandbox","svc-urlscan") and DeviceName !in~ ("SOC-SANDBOX01","PROXY-SCAN01")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the host/user and the initiating process from DeviceNetworkEvents — confirm it was a browser/mail client (real user) vs a sandbox/proxy host, and whether a file download or credential-entry POST followed within 5 min. 2) CONTAIN: sinkhole/block the domain at DNS and the secure web gateway tenant-wide; if the user submitted data, force a password reset + revoke sessions and isolate the host if a payload landed. 3) HUNT: pivot on the resolved IP and registrar pattern (.top, GoDaddy/Hostinger/Namecheap/Porkbun/IONOS) to surface sibling FIFA lookalikes the same host or org touched; review EmailEvents for the delivering message.

Inbound mail or embedded URL from FIFA 2026 impersonation domains AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound email whose sender domain (envelope or header-from) or embedded URL belongs to the FIFA World Cup 2026 fraud domains — the article notes a subset have MX records configured for reply-path impersonation and password-reset interception. Article-specific via the named domains rather than a generic spoofing rule. Rationale: Anchors on the same seven named fraud domains but on the mail vector (SenderFromDomain / SenderMailFromDomain / embedded URL), targeting the reply-path-impersonation and password-reset-interception use the article calls out for the MX-enabled subset. Domains corroborated by FBI IC3 and Check Point; mail tracing is uniquely a Defender-for-O365 signal, so other platforms are left blank. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260527 • https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/before-the-first-whistle-how-cyber-criminals-are-targeting-world-cup-2026/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal phishing-simulation platform using a FIFA-themed lure domain that overlaps a string
  • Brand-protection vendor sending sample/takedown-notice mail referencing the domains
  • Threat-intel newsletter or this very article being forwarded internally with the domains in the body (URL match on a benign report)
  • Quarantined/blocked messages surfacing in the hunt even though they never reached a user (DeliveryAction = Blocked/Quarantine)
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryLocation in ("Inbox","JunkFolder") and SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourphishsimvendor.com"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation — prioritize messages Delivered to Inbox; check whether the recipient clicked (UrlClickEvents) or replied. 2) CONTAIN: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide via Explorer, block the sender domain and embedded URL, and if any recipient entered credentials or replied to a reply-path lure, force password reset + revoke tokens. 3) HUNT: search for the same sender infrastructure (shared IP/SPF record) hitting other mailboxes and correlate recipients against the UC1 network/DNS hits to find users who both received and visited the domain.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

SimpleHelp CVE-2026-48558 forged OIDC Technician self-registration AIExploitation High
Hunts the server-side footprint of the SimpleHelp OIDC authentication bypass (CVE-2026-48558): an unauthenticated attacker forges an OIDC token and the SimpleHelp server logs a brand-new 'Technician' account registration. Surfaces the registered technician identity so analysts can compare it against the known technician roster. Rationale: Uses the exact SimpleHelp server.log strings Horizon3.ai published for CVE-2026-48558 ('Registering technician login for', 'Configuration save requested') — these are emitted on the OIDC token-forgery account creation and are the earliest detectable exploit artifact. SPL is a raw log search (no CIM datamodel covers SimpleHelp app logs). Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1190 T1606
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of a new technician/contractor via OIDC SSO
  • Admin testing or migrating the OIDC/Azure AD IdP configuration
  • MSP adding a new analyst account during shift handover
  • SimpleHelp version upgrade re-registering existing technicians
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the RegisteredTechnician value and compare against the approved technician roster; check the IdP for a matching real user and the source IP of the registration. 2) Contain: if the technician is unrecognised, disable/delete the account in SimpleHelp, revoke its sessions, and block the source IP; confirm the server is patched to the fixed SimpleHelp build. 3) Hunt: review server.log for scripts/files pushed by that technician and pivot to managed endpoints for node.exe/jquery.js execution (TaskWeaver).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has "Registering technician login for" or SyslogMessage has "Configuration save requested"
| extend RegisteredTechnician = extract(@"Registering technician login for\s+([^\s""']+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, RegisteredTechnician, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog ("Registering technician login for" OR "Configuration save requested")
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype="simplehelp:server" "Registering technician login for"
| rex "Registering technician login for\s+(?<registered_technician>[^\s\"']+)"
| table _time host registered_technician _raw
| sort - _time
SimpleHelp Remote Access process spawning Node.js / script interpreters AIExploitation High
Detects the SimpleHelp endpoint agent ('Remote Access.exe' / 'remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe') spawning script interpreters or LOLBins on a managed host — the post-exploitation execution channel a forged Technician uses to drop TaskWeaver. Article-specific because TaskWeaver runs via node.exe pushed through the trusted RMM channel. Rationale: SimpleHelp's confirmed endpoint binary names ('Remote Access.exe', 'remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe') as parent of interpreters captures the trusted-RMM command-execution channel the article describes ('transferring files and executing commands on systems managed through the server'). node.exe is included because TaskWeaver runs via node.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa25-163a • https://forums.malwarebytes.com/topic/303064-simplehelp-remoteaccesswinlauncherexe-false-positive/
ATT&CKT1219 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Technician running cmd/powershell interactively for legitimate remote support
  • RMM-pushed patching/automation scripts (powershell/cmd) during maintenance windows
  • A legitimately RMM-deployed Node.js application or installer
  • certutil/curl used by IT for legitimate file transfer during a support session
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("jquery.js","-enc","-EncodedCommand","FromBase64String","\\AppData\\","\\Temp\\","\\Public\\") or FileName =~ "node.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — benign support uses readable commands; flag obfuscated/base64 cmdlines or node.exe loading a .js from temp/AppData. Confirm the initiating technician is approved (cross-ref UC1). 2) Contain: if malicious, isolate the host, kill the process tree, and suspend the SimpleHelp technician account driving the session. 3) Hunt: search the same device for node.exe executing jquery.js, outbound dev-tunnels.com, and connections to 96.126.130.126:58942.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe","RemoteAccess.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe","RemoteAccess.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SimpleHelp Remote Access Process Spawning Script Interpreter
id: 7c1e6a52-4b8f-4d3a-9b21-3e1c0a9f2d11
status: experimental
description: Detects the SimpleHelp endpoint agent spawning script interpreters or LOLBins, as seen in CVE-2026-48558 exploitation to deploy TaskWeaver.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\Remote Access.exe'
      - '\remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe'
      - '\RemoteAccess.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'

      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\Remote\ Access.exe OR *\\remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe OR *\\RemoteAccess.exe) @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/remote ?access(winlauncher)?\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(node|cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|bitsadmin|certutil|curl)\.exe$/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe","RemoteAccess.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("node.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe","RemoteAccess.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("node.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| sort - lastTime
TaskWeaver loader: node.exe executing jquery.js AIInstallation High
Hunts the TaskWeaver Node.js loader, which the article states is 'delivered as jquery.js and executed through node.exe'. A Node runtime executing a script masquerading as the browser jQuery library is a high-fidelity, attack-specific signal. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's loader description: TaskWeaver 'delivered as jquery.js and executed through node.exe'. jQuery is a browser-side library, so a node.exe command line referencing jquery.js is anomalous and campaign-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer with an unusual build/test script literally named jquery.js run under Node (rare)
  • An npm package whose test harness references a file named jquery.js
  • Server-side rendering frameworks bundling a file path containing 'jquery.js'
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\","\\Public\\","\\ProgramData\\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture FolderPath/SHA256 of node.exe and the jquery.js location; legitimate hits resolve under a project/node_modules tree, malicious ones run from temp/AppData/Public or via the RMM session. 2) Contain: isolate the host, collect the jquery.js file, kill node.exe, and submit the hash for blocking. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same node.exe PID/host for outbound dev-tunnels.com beacons and exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942, and check the parent for SimpleHelp Remote Access.exe.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TaskWeaver Node.js Loader Executing jquery.js

TaskWeaver C2 beacon to dev-tunnels.com from node.exe AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the TaskWeaver C2 channel: node.exe resolving/connecting to a.dev-tunnels.com (Microsoft Dev Tunnels abused for C2). Scoped to a node.exe initiator to separate malicious tunneling from legitimate developer Dev Tunnels usage. Rationale: Uses the article's named C2 host (a.dev-tunnels.com) constrained to a node.exe initiator (TaskWeaver runtime). Dev Tunnels is a legitimate Microsoft service, so process scoping is required; Sentinel DnsEvents cannot attribute process, so confidence is Medium there. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers using Microsoft Dev Tunnels for legitimate port forwarding from VS/VS Code (which uses Node-based tooling)
  • CI/CD agents creating dev tunnels for remote debugging
  • Node-based local web apps exposed via Dev Tunnels for testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the node.exe is a known dev workflow vs. the jquery.js loader (cross-ref UC3) and review the InitiatingProcessCommandLine. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed-dev, isolate host, block the dev-tunnels subdomain at the proxy, and kill node.exe. 3) Hunt: check the host for jquery.js execution, SimpleHelp Remote Access.exe parentage, and follow-on exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "dev-tunnels.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Name has "dev-tunnels.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, IPAddresses, QueryTypeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TaskWeaver C2 - node.exe Querying dev-tunnels.com

Djinn Stealer multi-store credential harvesting by node.exe AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Djinn Stealer second stage: the TaskWeaver node.exe runtime touching files across multiple distinct credential classes (cloud CLI, SSH/GPG keys, infra tooling, AI-assistant configs, crypto wallets) in a short window. The cross-class fan-out (>=3 categories) is the behavioural signature the article enumerates. Rationale: Encodes the article's explicit target list for Djinn Stealer (AWS/Azure/GCP/OCI configs, SSH keys, Docker/Helm/Vault, npm/pnpm, AI-assistant configs for Claude/Gemini/Codex, crypto wallets). Requiring node.exe to touch >=3 distinct credential classes turns a noisy file-access query into a stealer-fan-out signal. No Sigma (threshold/correlation); Datadog omitted as auditd schema here lacks a reliable file-path facet for credential reads. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1555 T1552.001 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based dev tooling legitimately reading cloud creds (serverless framework, aws-cdk, pulumi, wrangler) on a developer workstation
  • Dotfile-sync or backup agents enumerating home-directory config
  • An IaC pipeline node process reading .terraform/.kube/.docker during a deploy
  • IDE extensions (VS Code, run via Node) indexing project credential files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review SampleFiles/Categories — a genuine dev tool stays within one ecosystem (e.g. only .aws), while Djinn spans cloud+keys+ai+wallet; confirm node.exe lineage (jquery.js / SimpleHelp parent). 2) Contain: isolate the host and treat every touched credential as compromised — rotate cloud keys, SSH/GPG keys, npm/registry tokens, AI-assistant API keys, and sweep wallets. 3) Hunt: look for a TAR/GZIP staging file written by node.exe and outbound transfer to 96.126.130.126:58942; expand credential rotation to any production systems reachable with the stolen keys.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.aws", @"\.azure", @"\.config\gcloud", @"\.oci", @"\.ssh", @"\.docker", @"\.kube", @"\.config\gh", @"\.gnupg", @"\.npmrc", @"\.config\helm", @"\.vault-token", @"\.claude", @"\.config\anthropic", @"\.gemini", @"\.codeium", @"\.electrum", @"\Login Data", @"wallet.dat")
| extend CredCategory = case(
    FolderPath has @"\.aws" or FolderPath has @"\.azure" or FolderPath has @"\.config\gcloud" or FolderPath has @"\.oci", "cloud",
    FolderPath has @"\.ssh" or FolderPath has @"\.gnupg", "keys",
    FolderPath has @"\.docker" or FolderPath has @"\.kube" or FolderPath has @"\.config\helm" or FolderPath has @"\.vault-token", "infra",
    FolderPath has @"\.claude" or FolderPath has @"\.config\anthropic" or FolderPath has @"\.gemini" or FolderPath has @"\.codeium", "ai",
    FolderPath has @"\.electrum" or FolderPath has @"wallet.dat", "wallet",
    FolderPath has @"\Login Data", "browser",
    "other")
| summarize DistinctCategories = dcount(CredCategory), Categories = make_set(CredCategory), FilesTouched = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FolderPath, 20), StartTime = min(Timestamp), EndTime = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where DistinctCategories >= 3
| order by EndTime desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.aws", @"\.azure", @"\.config\gcloud", @"\.oci", @"\.ssh", @"\.docker", @"\.kube", @"\.config\gh", @"\.gnupg", @"\.npmrc", @"\.vault-token", @"\.claude", @"\.config\anthropic", @"\.gemini", @"\.electrum", @"\Login Data", @"wallet.dat")
| summarize FilesTouched = dcount(TargetFilePath), SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFilePath, 20), StartTime = min(TimeGenerated), EndTime = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where FilesTouched >= 4
| order by EndTime desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\(\\.aws|\\.azure|\\.ssh|\\.docker|\\.kube|\\.gnupg|gcloud|\\.oci|\\.claude|\\.gemini|\\.electrum|\\.vault-token)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=DistinctFiles))
| DistinctFiles >= 4

Djinn Stealer exfiltration to 96.126.130.126:58942 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the encrypted-archive exfiltration step: an outbound connection to the attacker IP 96.126.130.126 on TCP port 58942, where Djinn Stealer ships the AES-256-GCM/RSA-2048-encrypted TAR.GZ of harvested credentials. The exact IP+non-standard-port pair is the article's hardest IOC. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exfil endpoint (96.126.130.126:58942). The IP+uncommon-port pair is highly specific; the Defender/Falcon variants also surface the initiating process so analysts can confirm it is the node.exe/Djinn runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1571 T1560.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Highly unlikely for this exact IP+port; possible only if a benign internal service is later assigned 96.126.130.126 (a Linode-range IP)
  • An internet-wide scanner or threat-intel sensor in your org deliberately probing the IOC
  • Penetration-test/purple-team replaying the IOC during an authorized exercise
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and InitiatingProcessFileName; any hit is treated as confirmed exfil given the IOC specificity — estimate bytes_out/NetworkBytes to gauge data volume. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 96.126.130.126 (and the /24) at the egress firewall, and kill the responsible process. 3) Hunt: assume credentials enumerated by Djinn (UC5) are exfiltrated — force org-wide rotation of cloud/SSH/registry/AI keys, hunt other hosts beaconing to the same IP, and review SimpleHelp for additional compromised endpoints.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP == "96.126.130.126" and RemotePort == 58942
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr == "96.126.130.126" and DstPortNumber == 58942
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkBytes, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

BleepingComputer

American insurance giant Aflac has disclosed a new data breach after attackers breached its Japan subsidiary's systems and stole personal and bank account information. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"

| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData

OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
