   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-06-30 11 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An in-depth analysis of Umbrij, a new tool used by the ToddyCat APT group to compromise corporate email communications in Gmail. The attack targeted OAuth authorization tokens, allowing threat actors to gain access to Google services.

ATT&CKT1027 T1053.005 T1134.003 T1190 T1204.002 T1528 T1574.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) · [LLM] Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary · [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence/launch step where ToddyCat created a scheduled task named KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp to run a digitally-signed sideload host. Kaspersky never creates a task with this name, so any occurrence of the string is malicious by definition. Rationale: Anchors on the exact masquerading task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' called out in the article's Execution section; it is a fixed, unique string no legitimate product emits. Cross-checked Securelist part 2 and the ToddyCat series. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-steals-email-data-from-outlook/118044/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A SOC analyst manually re-creating the task name during IR reproduction/testing
  • An internal red-team emulating ToddyCat TTPs
  • A detection-content lab importing the IOC string into a test task
  • Documentation/scripts that reference the task name in comments being scanned by inventory tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the scheduled task definition (Actions/Exec path) and the signed binary it launches; verify the signer and whether the path is a writable dir (Users\Public, Temp, vss). 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and capture the launched binary + any same-folder DLL for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the launched binary hash and folder across the fleet; check for the BDS.exe/log.dll sideload chain and Chromium remote-debugging launches on the same host within +/- 1h.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ProcessCommandLine has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName),
(DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RegistryKey has @"\TaskCache\" and RegistryKey has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=RegistryKey, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4698, 4702, 4699)
| where EventData has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Activity, EventID, EventData
title: Masquerading Scheduled Task KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp (ToddyCat Umbrij)
id: 6f3a1d2e-9b7c-4e10-8a44-2c1f0b9d7e51
description: Detects creation or reference to a scheduled task named KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp, a name ToddyCat used to masquerade Umbrij launch. Kaspersky does not create tasks with this name.

  - attack.t1036.004

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i | CommandLine=/KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name

ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact sideload pairs ToddyCat abused to launch Umbrij: BDSubWiz.exe/bds.exe loading log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder.exe loading Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll, and GoogleDesktop.exe loading GoogleServices.dll, when the module loads from a user-writable directory or matches the known log.dll hashes. Rationale: Uses the exact legitimate-host -> malicious-DLL pairs named in the article (BDSubWiz/bds.exe+log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder+VideoRecorderEngine.dll, GoogleDesktop+GoogleServices.dll), plus the writable paths and log.dll/BDS.exe MD5s read directly from in-article screenshot image1.jpeg (4C39087.../22AAEB49... and 28CB7B26...). Writable-path constraint removes legitimate in-product loads. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Bitdefender ConnectAgent running BDSubWiz.exe from its real Program Files path (excluded by writable-path filter)
  • Visual Studio test runs loading VideoRecorderEngine.dll from the VS install directory
  • A legacy Google Desktop install in Program Files loading GoogleServices.dll
  • Security testing/EDR validation copying these binaries into a sandbox temp folder
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded DLL hash against the known IOCs and verify the host binary is running from Users\Public/Temp/vss rather than its vendor install path; check the DLL export (LogInit) and ConfuserEx markers. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the DLL and host binary, kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: from the host process, pivot to child Chromium launches with --remote-debugging-port and outbound connections to *.googleapis.com; sweep fleet for the same DLL hashes and the KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe") and FileName =~ "log.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and FileName =~ "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FileName =~ "GoogleServices.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
     or MD5 in~ ("4C39087E5229A70F0215AFB8B7083091","22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, Dll=FileName, DllPath=FolderPath, MD5, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(BDSubWiz|bds|VSTestVideoRecorder|GoogleDesktop)\.exe$/i | (ImageFileName=/\\(Users\\Public|Temp|vss)\\/i OR MD5HashData=/^28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1$/i) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, MD5HashData], function=count())

Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the Umbrij tool by its distinctive command-line parameters documented in the article, including the example invocation of a renamed BDSubWiz.exe with -regex and -deepsearch. These switch names are unique to Umbrij. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim Umbrij CLI parameters enumerated in the article's parameter table (-deepsearch, -runas-currentuser, -domainAd, -savepdf, -debugport, -browser). These switch spellings are tool-specific and not used by mainstream software, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1528 T1134.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bespoke internal automation tool that happens to use a -debugport plus -browser flag combination
  • Red-team replaying Umbrij invocations during an authorized engagement
  • An unrelated CLI utility using the generic -savepdf flag (mitigated by requiring the ToddyCat-specific switch set)
  • Developer testing of a custom .NET tool with similar argument naming
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the executing binary; resolve which browser/path/port were targeted (-path, -browser, -debugport) and whether -runas-currentuser/-user indicates token impersonation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and revoke/rotate the affected user's Google OAuth sessions and tokens immediately. 3) Hunt: correlate with the parent sideload host (BDS.exe/log.dll), Chromium --remote-debugging-port launches, and outbound *.googleapis.com traffic on the same host and account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "-debugport" and ProcessCommandLine has "-browser")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (CommandLine has "-debugport" and CommandLine has "-browser")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-deepsearch'
      - '-runas-currentuser'
      - '-domainAd'
      - '-savepdf'
  debug_browser:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '-debugport'
      - '-browser'
  condition: unique_switches or debug_browser
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@CommandLine:(*-deepsearch* OR *-runas-currentuser* OR *-domainAd* OR *-savepdf*) OR (@CommandLine:*-debugport* AND @CommandLine:*-browser*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (CommandLine=/-deepsearch/i OR CommandLine=/-runas-currentuser/i OR CommandLine=/-domainAd/i OR CommandLine=/-savepdf/i OR (CommandLine=/-debugport/i AND CommandLine=/-browser/i)) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*-deepsearch*" OR Processes.process="*-runas-currentuser*" OR Processes.process="*-domainAd*" OR Processes.process="*-savepdf*" OR (Processes.process="*-debugport*" AND Processes.process="*-browser*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*-deepsearch*" OR Processes.process="*-runas-currentuser*" OR Processes.process="*-domainAd*" OR Processes.process="*-savepdf*" OR (Processes.process="*-debugport*" AND Processes.process="*-browser*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core Shadow-Token-via-Remote-Debug step: Umbrij launches Chrome/Edge/Chromium with a remote debugging port (often headless) to drive the user's live Gmail session. Flags browser processes carrying --remote-debugging-port when spawned by the sideload hosts or run headless. Rationale: Built on the article's explicit description of launching a Chromium browser in headless mode and connecting via the remote debugging port; pairs the --remote-debugging-port flag with the article-specific sideload parents or the --headless evasion flag to suppress legitimate interactive debugging. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1185 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/QA running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright automation with --remote-debugging-port and --headless
  • CI build agents driving headless Chrome for screenshot or PDF generation
  • VS Code / IDE debugging a web app via the Chrome DevTools Protocol
  • Synthetic monitoring agents launching headless browsers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft VS Code" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","devenv.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and folder — a CI/automation tool from a dev path is likely benign; a browser spawned by BDSubWiz/bds/GoogleDesktop or from Users\Public/Temp is malicious. Note the --remote-debugging-port value and target profile. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the browser and parent, and immediately revoke the user's Google sessions/refresh tokens and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com connections from the same host/account and to the Umbrij CLI-switch and log.dll sideload detections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\chrome.exe", @"\msedge.exe", @"\chromium.exe", @"\brave.exe")
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or CommandLine has "--headless"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Chromium Remote Debugging Port Launch by Non-Browser Parent (ToddyCat STRD)
id: 4a8c6b29-1e57-4d33-9b2a-0f7e5c3a1d92
description: Detects Chrome/Edge/Chromium launched with --remote-debugging-port either headless or spawned by a ToddyCat sideload-host binary, the core of the Shadow Token via Remote Debug technique.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1185
  - attack.t1528
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  browser_debug:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\chromium.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '--remote-debugging-port'
  suspicious_context:
    - CommandLine|contains: '--headless'
    - ParentImage|endswith:
        - '\BDSubWiz.exe'
        - '\bds.exe'
        - '\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe'
        - '\GoogleDesktop.exe'
  condition: browser_debug and suspicious_context
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\MSEdge.exe OR *\\chromium.exe)) @CommandLine:*--remote-debugging-port* (@CommandLine:*--headless* OR @ParentImage:(*\\BDS.exe OR *\\bds.exe OR *\\BDSubWiz.exe OR *\\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe OR *\\GoogleDesktop.exe))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|chromium|brave)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/--remote-debugging-port/i | (CommandLine=/--headless/i OR ParentBaseFileName=/(BDSubWiz|bds|VSTestVideoRecorder|GoogleDesktop)\.exe$/i) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="chrome.exe" OR Processes.process_name="msedge.exe" OR Processes.process_name="chromium.exe") AND Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" AND (Processes.process="*--headless*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="BDSubWiz.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="bds.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="GoogleDesktop.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="chrome.exe" OR Processes.process_name="msedge.exe" OR Processes.process_name="chromium.exe") AND Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" AND (Processes.process="*--headless*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="BDSubWiz.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="bds.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="GoogleDesktop.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access/exfil step where Umbrij (running as a renamed signed binary, not a browser) exchanges the stolen OAuth authorization code for an access token and pulls Gmail via the Google API. Flags the sideload hosts contacting *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com. Rationale: Combines the article's OAuth-code-to-access-token exchange and Google-API access with the sideload host names confirmed in screenshot image1.jpeg; a renamed Bitdefender/VSTest/GoogleDesktop binary speaking directly to Google OAuth/Gmail APIs (work normally done only by the browser) is a strong, low-FP anomaly. Sentinel left empty because process-attributed network telemetry to these hosts is not available in standard Sentinel tables (would require Sysmon EID3 ingestion). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1528 T1114.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Google Desktop legacy install (in Program Files) performing update/sync checks to googleapis.com
  • Bitdefender ConnectAgent telemetry/update traffic to a Google-hosted CDN (rare; mitigated by host-name + writable-path context)
  • Security testing of the binaries in a lab with live internet
  • A renamed-but-benign internal tool reusing one of these file names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary path/signer and verify it is the renamed sideload host rather than the genuine vendor product; pull the destination URLs and timing relative to any browser remote-debug launch. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the binary, and revoke the affected Google account's OAuth tokens/refresh tokens and active sessions; review Google Workspace audit logs for token grants and bulk message reads. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts where these binaries reach Google APIs, correlate with the log.dll sideload and KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task, and check for mailbox data staged/exfiltrated.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ToddyCat Sideload Host Contacting Google OAuth/Gmail API
id: e7b3c91d-5a42-4f8e-8c01-9d2f6a3b7e58
description: Detects a ToddyCat sideload-host binary (not a browser) making network connections to Google OAuth / Gmail API endpoints, indicating OAuth token exchange and remote mailbox access.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1528
  - attack.t1114.002
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\BDSubWiz.exe'
      - '\bds.exe'
      - '\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe'
      - '\GoogleDesktop.exe'
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'googleapis.com'
      - 'accounts.google.com'
      - 'oauth2.googleapis.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\\BDS.exe OR *\\bds.exe OR *\\BDSubWiz.exe OR *\\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe OR *\\GoogleDesktop.exe)) (@DestinationHostname:(*googleapis.com OR *accounts.google.com))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(googleapis\.com|accounts\.google\.com|oauth2\.googleapis\.com)/i | ContextImageFileName=/\\(BDSubWiz|bds|VSTestVideoRecorder|GoogleDesktop)\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="BDSubWiz.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bds.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="GoogleDesktop.exe") AND (All_Traffic.dest="*googleapis.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest="*accounts.google.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="BDSubWiz.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bds.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="GoogleDesktop.exe") AND (All_Traffic.dest="*googleapis.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest="*accounts.google.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Blackfield (BlackFL) ransomware encryption: .BlackFL extension + BlackField_ReadMe.txt note drop AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the file-system signature of Blackfield/BlackFL ransomware encryption: files renamed/created with the unique '.BlackFL' extension and the dropping of the 'BlackField_ReadMe.txt' (or Feb-2026 variant 'BlackField-ReadMe.txt') ransom note. Both strings are unique to this family — corroborated across PCrisk, EnigmaSoft and WatchGuard — so this is article/campaign-specific rather than a generic mass-rename heuristic. Rationale: Anchored on two strings unique to this family and confirmed by second sources (PCrisk, WatchGuard): the '.BlackFL' encrypted-file extension and the 'BlackField_ReadMe.txt'/'BlackField-ReadMe.txt' ransom note. Neither appears in benign software, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware • https://www.watchguard.com/wgrd-security-hub/ransomware-tracker/blackfield • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or researcher host holding sample files that already carry the '.BlackFL' extension
  • A security awareness/IR test or purple-team exercise intentionally dropping a file named BlackField_ReadMe.txt
  • Backup or quarantine archive that preserved previously-encrypted '.BlackFL' files being restored to a host
  • A threat-intel document or zip containing the ransom note text saved with the literal note filename
Suppression filter
| where AffectedFolders >= 2 or RansomNoteDropped >= 1   // single isolated .BlackFL sample with no note is likely a researcher/backup artifact
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the alerting DeviceName, pull the InitiatingProcess/SHA256 that wrote the files and check whether '.BlackFL' files span multiple folders (mass-rename = live encryption vs. a single benign sample). Confirm the BlackField_ReadMe.txt note timestamp. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately network-isolate the host via EDR, suspend/kill the initiating process, and disable the involved account; preserve a memory image before reimaging. 3) HUNT: Pivot the initiating-process SHA256 and the writing account across all hosts; search for the WMIC shadow-copy deletion (UC2), recent SMB share enumeration, and lateral logons from the same account to scope blast radius across the Nidec Chaun Choung subnet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".BlackFL"
    or FileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"
| summarize EncryptedFileCount = countif(FileName endswith ".BlackFL"),
            RansomNoteDropped = countif(FileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"),
            AffectedFolders = dcount(FolderPath),
            SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 8),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            InitiatingProcess = any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            InitiatingProcessSHA256 = any(InitiatingProcessSHA256),
            InitiatingCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
        by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId
| where EncryptedFileCount >= 1 or RansomNoteDropped >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".BlackFL"
    or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"
| summarize EncryptedFileCount = countif(TargetFileName endswith ".BlackFL"),
            RansomNoteDropped = countif(TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"),
            AffectedPaths = dcount(TargetFilePath),
            SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 8),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Process = any(ActingProcessName)
        by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId
| where EncryptedFileCount >= 1 or RansomNoteDropped >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Blackfield (BlackFL) Ransomware Encryption Artifacts
id: 7c2f1e84-3b6a-4d2e-9f10-2a1b9c8d4e51
description: Detects file-system artifacts of Blackfield/BlackFL ransomware - files renamed/created with the .BlackFL extension or the BlackField_ReadMe.txt ransom note being dropped.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
  - https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1486
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.BlackFL'
  selection_note:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - 'BlackField_ReadMe.txt'
      - 'BlackField-ReadMe.txt'
  condition: selection_ext or selection_note
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*.BlackFL OR *.blackfl OR *.BLACKFL) OR @TargetFilename:(*\\BlackField_ReadMe.txt OR *\\BlackField-ReadMe.txt OR *\\blackfield_readme.txt))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\.BlackFL$|BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt$)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| count >= 1
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path dc(Filesystem.file_path) as folder_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.BlackFL" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField_ReadMe.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField-ReadMe.txt") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path dc(Filesystem.file_path) as folder_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.BlackFL" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField_ReadMe.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField-ReadMe.txt") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
Blackfield ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via WMIC (inhibit recovery) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the pre-encryption recovery-inhibition step documented for Blackfield/BlackFL: use of WMIC.exe to delete Volume Shadow Copies (with vssadmin as a fallback variant). Pairs with the encryption UC to give execution + impact coverage of the same intrusion before files are locked. Rationale: BlackField is documented (PCrisk/SOCRadar) to terminate recovery options by using WMIC.exe to delete Volume Shadow Copies; the wmic shadowcopy-delete and vssadmin delete-shadows command shapes are the concrete invocations. Medium fidelity because legitimate backup tooling can issue similar commands, hence the FP filter. Cross-checked against: • https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware • https://www.ransomware.live/group/Blackfield • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
ATT&CKT1490 T1047
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam / Acronis / Commvault backup jobs running pre-snapshot shadow-copy cleanup
  • Sysadmin manually troubleshooting VSS (vssadmin list/delete shadows) during storage maintenance
  • Windows imaging or DISM operations recycling shadow storage
  • SQL Server / Exchange backup maintenance scripts invoking WMIC shadowcopy operations
  • Endpoint management/SCCM task that prunes shadow copies on a schedule
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","veeam.backup.manager.exe","acronis.exe","clussvc.exe","vsnapvss.exe","ccmexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the parent process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a backup product (veeam, acronis) or services.exe-spawned admin tool is likely benign; an unsigned/unusual parent or one running from a temp path is high-risk. Check the same host for '.BlackFL' files (UC1). 2) CONTAIN: If the parent is not an approved backup agent, isolate the host immediately and disable the executing account before encryption completes. 3) HUNT: Sweep all hosts for the same parent SHA256, recent backup-deletion or bcdedit recovery-tampering commands, and the BlackField ransom note; review the account's logon history for lateral movement into the affected subsidiary network.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "shadowcopy" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete")
    or (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Blackfield Ransomware Volume Shadow Copy Deletion via WMIC
id: 2d9a7f3c-1e4b-4a8d-bc60-5f3e2d1a9b74
description: Detects WMIC.exe (with vssadmin fallback) deleting Volume Shadow Copies, the documented recovery-inhibition step of Blackfield/BlackFL ransomware prior to encryption.
references:
  - https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1490
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1047
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_wmic:
    Image|endswith: '\wmic.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'shadowcopy'
      - 'delete'
  selection_vss:
    Image|endswith: '\vssadmin.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'delete'
      - 'shadows'
  condition: selection_wmic or selection_vss
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\\wmic.exe OR *\\WMIC.exe OR *\\WMIC.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*shadowcopy* AND *delete*)) OR (@Image:(*\\vssadmin.exe OR *\\VSSADMIN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*delete* AND *shadows*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(wmic|vssadmin)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/shadow/i
| CommandLine=/delete/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*") OR (Processes.process_name="vssadmin.exe" AND Processes.process="*delete*" AND Processes.process="*shadows*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*") OR (Processes.process_name="vssadmin.exe" AND Processes.process="*delete*" AND Processes.process="*shadows*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AirDrop and Quick Share Flaws Let Nearby Attackers Trigger Crashes and Bypass Checks

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 7 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Two researchers have found six security flaws in AirDrop and Quick Share, the wireless features that beam files between nearby devices with no cables or shared network. An attacker within wireless range, with just a laptop and no prior connection, can crash the sharing service on a Mac or iPhone set to receive from anyone, with no tap or prompt. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) spawning shell or LOLBin — UAF code execution · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) repeated crash/restart loop — UAF DoS · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) repeated crash/restart loop — UAF DoS AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the Google Quick Share for Windows client (nearby_share.exe) crashing and restarting repeatedly on a single host, consistent with a nearby/same-LAN attacker repeatedly colliding two connections to trigger the use-after-free described in the CISPA research. A persistent tray app restarting 5+ times in 10 minutes is not normal lifecycle behaviour. Rationale: Uses the concrete Windows Quick Share client binary name (nearby_share.exe, publisher Google LLC) confirmed via the SpyShelter process DB, plus the article's claim of a crash triggered when two connections collide. A persistent tray app restarting 5+ times / crashing repeatedly is the observable footprint of the local UAF DoS. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/apple-airdrop-google-samsung-quick-share-vulnerabilities/ • https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1 • https://www.spyshelter.com/exe/google-llc-nearby_share-exe/
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine app instability after a Windows feature update or a corrupt Quick Share install causing repeated WER crashes
  • User repeatedly relaunching Quick Share manually from the system tray after it hangs on a large legitimate transfer
  • Quick Share auto-update mid-session restarting the client process several times
  • Driver/Wi-Fi adapter resets on the host destabilising the Bluetooth+Wi-Fi stack Quick Share depends on
  • Sysmon/Defender double-reporting the same process start during high event volume
Suppression filter
// Suppress benign updater-driven restarts
| where SampleFolder !has "\\Update\\" and SampleCompany has_any ("Google", "")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host actually has Quick Share for Windows installed and pull the bin(10m) of nearby_share.exe starts / Application Error 1000 events; check whether the device was in a crowded shared space (airport/conference/office Wi-Fi) at crash time and whether CFG is enforced on the binary. 2) CONTAIN: Have the user close Quick Share and set visibility off 'Everyone' (out of receive mode); if the crash loop persists, isolate the host's Wi-Fi/Bluetooth or network-isolate and ensure the Google-patched Quick Share build is installed. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC 'nearby_share.exe spawning a shell/LOLBin' on the same host/time window to rule out the crash being escalated to code execution, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the inbound peer IP that preceded the crashes.
// Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) crash-restart loop — sustained proximity/LAN UAF DoS
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName =~ "nearby_share.exe"
| summarize LaunchCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleFolder = any(FolderPath), SampleCompany = any(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
        by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where LaunchCount >= 5   // >=5 (re)starts of the Quick Share tray app in 10 min = crash loop; normal lifecycle is 1 start per logon
| order by LastSeen desc
// Application Error (Event ID 1000) faulting on nearby_share.exe (Quick Share for Windows)
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where Source == "Application Error" and EventID == 1000
| where RenderedDescription has "nearby_share.exe"
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleDescription = any(RenderedDescription)
        by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CrashCount >= 3   // >=3 app-error crashes of Quick Share in 10 min
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\nearby_share.exe OR *\\Nearby_Share.exe OR *\\NEARBY_SHARE.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\nearby_share\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count())
| count >= 5
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="nearby_share.exe" by Processes.dest, Processes.user, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where count>=5
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="nearby_share.exe" by Processes.dest, Processes.user, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where count>=5
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) spawning shell or LOLBin — UAF code execution AIExploitation High
Hunts for the Quick Share for Windows client (nearby_share.exe) spawning a command shell, scripting host, or download-capable LOLBin as a child. The CISPA research notes the Windows use-after-free is plausibly exploitable for code execution because Control Flow Guard is disabled in the app; nearby_share.exe legitimately spawns no such children, so any is high-fidelity. Rationale: Grounded in the article's specific claim that the Windows Quick Share UAF is plausibly exploitable for code execution (CFG off). Uses the concrete parent binary nearby_share.exe; this tray app has no legitimate reason to spawn cmd/powershell/mshta/rundll32 etc., making the parent->child pair high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/apple-airdrop-google-samsung-quick-share-vulnerabilities/ • https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1 • https://www.spyshelter.com/exe/google-llc-nearby_share-exe/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Quick Share updater logic shelling out to a maintenance/cleanup script during an in-place upgrade
  • Enterprise software-management agent injecting a child process under nearby_share.exe for inventory
  • Security tooling (EDR/DLP) reparenting or hollowing nearby_share.exe causing an apparent child spawn
  • An IT helpdesk troubleshooting script launched while Quick Share happened to be the foreground process (rare reparent)
Suppression filter
// Drop known updater path if it legitimately invokes cmd in your environment
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Quick Share\\Update\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 — decode any encoded/obfuscated args, check the child's network connections and file writes, and confirm whether a Quick Share crash (UC1) or an inbound peer connection immediately preceded this on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and capture nearby_share.exe memory; block the child binary hash if attacker-supplied. 3) HUNT: Sweep the fleet for the same parent->child pair, pivot on the child's C2 destinations across DeviceNetworkEvents, and verify all endpoints run Google's patched Quick Share build.
// nearby_share.exe (Quick Share for Windows) spawning a shell/LOLBin child — possible UAF -> code execution
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nearby_share.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// 4688: nearby_share.exe spawning shell/LOLBin
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\nearby_share.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

CVE-2026-33825 (BlueHammer) exposure: unpatched Microsoft Defender engine AIExploitation High
Surfaces endpoints still vulnerable to the BlueHammer Defender LPE (CVE-2026-33825), a CISA-KEV ransomware-flagged flaw with a passed FCEB patch deadline. Exposure-management pivot to prioritise the Defender Antimalware Platform 4.18.26050.3011 update before the local-privesc primitive can be abused. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CVE (CVE-2026-33825) and the corroborated patched platform build 4.18.26050.3011; Defender TVM maps the CVE directly, so this is a high-fidelity exposure list. Pre-extracted MD5s were uncorroborated in any second source and excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/bluehammer-redsun-windows-defender-cve-2026-33825-zero-day-vulnerability-explained • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-33825 • https://github.com/fleetdm/fleet/issues/45633
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Devices already on Defender platform 4.18.26050.3011+ but with a stale TVM snapshot pending re-scan
  • Decommissioned or long-offline endpoints still present in inventory
  • Air-gapped hosts where Defender auto-update is deliberately disabled under compensating controls
  • Non-Windows assets mis-tagged in the vuln-scanner feed
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the device list and cross-check each against current Defender platform version (4.18.26050.3011+ is patched); drop hosts already updated. 2) Contain: force the Defender Antimalware Platform update on remaining hosts; for internet-facing or high-value systems apply attack-surface-reduction and restrict local logon until patched. 3) Hunt: for any host that stayed unpatched past the April patch window, pivot to UC2/UC3 (MsMpEng writes to System32 / MsMpEng child process) over the exposure window to confirm the primitive wasn't already abused.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-33825"
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-33825"
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
